items.text: Find the paper about saving hash-table space by allowing false positive membership tests.
Bloom filters trade a small false-positive rate for compact set-membership tests.

Burton Bloom's paper examines space and time costs in hash coding. It considers testing messages for membership in a stored set, especially when most messages are not members. Permitting some false positive answers can reduce the size of the hash area while keeping rejection fast. A more expensive secondary test can catch the occasional false match. The key trade-off is not exact lookup with less memory for free: an allowable error frequency becomes a third design parameter alongside space and rejection time. This is why compact probabilistic membership structures are useful in front of expensive storage lookups.
Which paper introduced a translation architecture based entirely on attention instead of recurrence or convolutions?
Attention Is All You Need introduced the Transformer, replacing recurrent translation models with attention.

The Transformer paper proposes a sequence transduction architecture built around attention. Previous strong translation systems relied on recurrent or convolutional encoders and decoders, often supplemented by attention between them. The new model dispenses with those recurrence and convolution mechanisms and uses attention throughout. This makes training more parallelizable. The abstract reports English-to-German and English-to-French machine translation results and contrasts model quality and training time with the previous systems. This note concerns the original architecture, not the later hybrid recurrent layers used by some modern language models.

Find the study connecting valence and arousal to expected free energy in an artificial agent's search task.
A circumplex model maps emotion onto valence and arousal signals derived from expected free energy.

The paper Free Energy in a Circumplex Model of Emotion extends active-inference accounts that emphasize valence alone. It treats emotions in a two-dimensional space of valence and arousal. In the proposed model, arousal relates to the entropy of posterior beliefs, while valence relates to utility minus expected utility. Artificial agents perform a search task, and changing their prior beliefs or the presence of the searched-for object changes the resulting emotional signals. The source page contains the paper title, author affiliations, and abstract. It is about modeling emotional states, not a claim that a similarity vector itself measures feelings.
Where is the chapter explaining symmetric feedback neural networks as associative, content-addressable memories?
Hopfield networks are symmetric feedback networks used for associative memory and optimization.

Chapter 42 of MacKay's book introduces Hopfield networks after studying individual neurons. It first distinguishes feedforward networks, whose connections form an acyclic graph, from feedback networks. A Hopfield network is a fully connected feedback network with symmetric weights: the connection from one neuron to another has the same weight as the reverse connection. The chapter gives two applications, associative memory and optimization, and begins its discussion of memory with Hebbian learning. A figure on the opening page compares a feedforward diagram with a feedback diagram. The page is distinct from the preceding postscript on supervised neural networks.
